analysis.one_liner: Charges the biggest fossil fuel companies up to $1 trillion for past emissions to fund climate disaster protection.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to three House committees in September 2024, it received no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2025, with 22 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have billed roughly $1 trillion, split among fossil fuel extraction and refining companies based on how much carbon dioxide their products released from 2000 to 2022, and put the money into a dedicated fund. That fund would pay for disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and community protection from floods, heat, and wildfires, with 40 percent reserved for communities hit hardest by pollution. It would not have replaced any company's other legal liabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities facing climate-driven disasters — floods, hurricanes, extreme heat, wildfires — would get a dedicated funding stream for recovery and resilience, including at least $15 billion a year for FEMA programs and $6 billion for Clean Air Act grants. Low-income communities, communities of color, and Tribal communities would get a guaranteed 40 percent share of the fund's spending. Taxpayers currently paying for disaster relief would see some of that burden shift to the companies whose products caused the emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a total tax of $1 trillion, apportioned among companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide released between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2022, with each company's share based on its emissions above the threshold.

Creates a Polluters Pay Climate Fund whose money can only be spent on climate resilience, adaptation, disaster response, and environmental justice — including not less than $15 billion a year for FEMA disaster response and resilience programs (with at least $3 billion for the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program) and not less than $6 billion for Clean Air Act climate-impact grants.

Reserves 40 percent of the fund's annual spending for investments that benefit environmental justice communities — communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that bear more pollution and climate harm.
Lets companies pay in 9 annual installments (20 percent first, then 10 percent each), and bars them from deducting the tax from their other income taxes.

Explicitly preserves all existing rights to sue fossil fuel companies under state and federal law for climate damage, deception, or failure to warn, and says fund payments cannot offset or reduce any court-awarded damages.

analysis.who_pays: The largest fossil fuel extraction and refining companies would owe shares of a $1 trillion assessment by September 30, 2025 (or in installments through 2033). Some of that cost could be passed through to consumers in the form of higher energy prices, and the companies would lose the ability to deduct it. Energy prices could also face pressure simply from the disruption of a levy of this size.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies, possibly energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The assessment is backward-looking: it bills companies for carbon dioxide released from 2000 to 2022, when that activity was legal, which the companies and their allies would challenge as an unlegislated retroactive penalty and could tie up in years of litigation.
Because the tax falls on fuel production, part of it could reach consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices, at least in the short run.
It is a one-time levy on past emissions, not a price on future pollution, so on its own it creates no ongoing incentive to reduce emissions.

It applies to foreign corporations doing business in the United States and to controlled groups treated as a single company, raising questions about international trade disputes and enforcement against complex corporate structures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and concrete: the bill's own findings cite at least $150 billion a year in climate disaster costs to the United States, and the fund would shift a trillion dollars of resilience and recovery spending onto the companies whose products account for the emissions. The main honest costs are the retroactive structure (a legal target) and the risk of price pass-through to consumers. On balance this is a straightforward transfer from a concentrated industry to a public fund for disaster protection, though its design would have invited a court fight.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them ever held a hearing or markup, so it never reached the House floor before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Polluters Pay Climate Fund Act of 2024 in the House on September 12, 2024, with 17 original cosponsors listed at introduction.

The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and additionally to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Energy and Commerce Committees, where its tax provisions would fall under Ways and Means.
22 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows no Republicans.

The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 — a bill introduced less than four months before the session ended with three committee referrals had essentially no window to move.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The fossil fuel companies that would have owed shares of a $1 trillion assessment are better off, and the roughly $150 billion a year in climate disaster costs the bill cited continues to be borne by taxpayers and disaster-affected communities.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies that avoided the assessment

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 12, 2024 and recruited 17 original cosponsors.

for.name: 22 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the tax (R-led majority)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral, so its central tax provision never advanced.

against.name: Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the provisions within their jurisdiction during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority control of committees and the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill and the majority-controlled committees gave it no consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill received no action under the Republican committee majority; there was never a roll call to measure the split.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal extraction and refining companies
industries.note: The bill would have imposed a $1 trillion assessment apportioned among companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2000–2022, with joint liability across controlled corporate groups and no tax deduction. That cost is precisely the money ordinary taxpayers and disaster-hit communities would have gained, so the industry's interest runs directly against the public's here.

industries.industry: Households and businesses that buy fuel and electricity
industries.note: Consumers would be the fund's main beneficiaries through disaster recovery and resilience spending, but fuel producers could pass part of the assessment through as higher energy prices in the short run.
